name: Beth Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Clearclaim, which makes software insurers use to handle car accident claims. I write the rules that decide what happens to a claim, like whether a cracked windscreen gets paid straight away or sent to a person to check. Mornings are usually meetings with the product people, afternoons are coding and testing. I like the puzzle of it. What wears me out is when a client changes their mind about a rule three times in a week.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sometimes. I use the assistant for writing database queries and for explaining old code, maybe a few times a week. I wait until a tool has proved itself on the team before I rely on it. I live with my boyfriend Marco, who's a cook at an Italian restaurant, and we're saving for a deposit on a house. We've got about four months of living costs put by, which is separate from the deposit pot, and that pot is growing slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that's a fairly normal picture. I could live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a useful tool that got oversold, like a lot of things. At work I'd say let's use it where it helps and stop pretending it does more. I wouldn't post much about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately my job feels fine in that world. The thing that bothers me is Marco's restaurant, which has had two quiet winters. If his hours get cut again, the deposit plan slows right down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep using the assistant for queries. I'd keep putting three hundred a month into the deposit pot. If Marco's hours drop, I'd move some of that into the everyday savings instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about money at home, not about AI. It's the house that keeps me up, not the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How far off is the deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three years at this rate. Saving for a house deposit feels like walking up a down escalator. House prices keep moving. Marco jokes that we'll buy when we're fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Marco say about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says no robot is going to make his carbonara. He's probably right for a while. He worries more about the owner selling up.

say: I'd say AI was a **useful tool** that got **oversold**.
At work I'd say use it where it helps and **stop pretending**.
think: I privately feel my **job is fine** in this world.
My real worry is Marco's **restaurant hours** and the house deposit.
do: Keep using the assistant for **database queries** at Clearclaim.
Keep putting **three hundred a month** into the deposit pot.
Shift deposit money into everyday savings if **Marco's hours** drop.
feel: She feels **uneasy** about money at home, not about AI.
S0.quote: Saving for a house deposit feels like walking up a down escalator.
fieldNote: Her unease comes from her **boyfriend's restaurant**, not from technology.
The **house deposit** is the centre of her plans in every scenario.
She is **practical** and reluctant to make public statements.

steps.text: Keep writing claims rules at Clearclaim and using AI for queries
Keep saving 300 a month toward the house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. Checking and coding. That's my whole job, really. Claims rules are a lot of checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to adapt sensibly, and that companies should train people rather than just cut. I'd say it calmly at work. I'd also say the insurers will want fewer people looking at claims, and that's going to hit the claims handlers before us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think AI could write most claims rules from the client's own documents. Our team of seven might be four in two years. I'm in the middle of the pack, so I'd have to make sure I was one of the four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the assistant every day once I'd seen it work on our rules, probably within a couple of months. I'd volunteer for the project where we test AI-written rules, so I'm the one checking it rather than the one replaced by it. And I'd hold off on the house for a year until things settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but manageable. It's like a storm forecast: you can't stop it, but you can bring the washing in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Holding off on the house is a big step. How did you get there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mortgage is twenty-five years, so I'd want to know my job is still there in two years before I sign. Marco would be disappointed, but he'd get it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if being the checker doesn't last either?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being the checker buys me a couple of years and some new skills. I'm not pretending it's forever. Nothing in software is forever.

say: I'd say companies should **train people** rather than just cut.
I'd point out the **claims handlers** at insurers get hit before developers.
think: I privately expect our team of **seven to become four**.
I'm in the **middle of the pack**, so I need to be one of the four.
do: Use the **assistant daily** once it proves itself on Clearclaim's rules.
Volunteer to **check AI-written rules** so she's the checker, not the replaced.
Put the **house purchase** on hold for a year.
feel: She feels **anxious** but manageable, like preparing for a **storm**.
S1.quote: A mortgage is twenty-five years, so I'd want to know my job is still there in two years before I sign.
fieldNote: She positions herself as the **checker** of AI work, a classic steady move.
The scenario pauses her **house plans** immediately.
She is realistic that this only **buys time**.

steps.text: Use the AI assistant daily once it works on Clearclaim's rules
Volunteer for the project checking AI-written claims rules
Put the house purchase on hold for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before we'd even have the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments and companies need to move fast on support, because this would hit everyone at once. I'd say it at work and with friends. I wouldn't be shouting, but I'd say it clearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd assume my job ends around 2028. Everything I do is screen work. Marco's kitchen work is hands-on, so he'd likely have a few more years than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house plan completely and put the deposit pot into savings, so we've got maybe ten months between us. I'd look at moving back to my parents' town, where rent is half. And I'd cut out the gym, the takeaways and the streaming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It would feel like the floor going. The deposit was the thing we were working toward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving back to your parents' town actually mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's an hour and a half away. Marco would need a new kitchen job, but restaurants are always hiring. We'd be closer to my mum, which she'd love and I'd find hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Marco the night you decided?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my boyfriend Marco the house isn't happening yet, and that it's not his fault or mine. Then I'd probably cry. Then we'd make a spreadsheet, because that's what I do.

say: I'd say governments and companies need to **move fast** on support.
I'd say it **clearly** but without shouting.
think: I privately assume my job ends around **2028**.
Marco's **kitchen work** is hands-on, so he'd likely last a few years longer.
do: Cancel the **house plan** and move the deposit into everyday savings.
Move to her **parents' town**, where rent is half.
feel: She feels **alarmed**, like the **floor going**, as the house goal disappears.
S2.quote: I'd tell my boyfriend Marco the house isn't happening yet, and that it's not his fault or mine.
fieldNote: The **deposit pot** becomes their emergency fund overnight.
Her boyfriend's **hands-on job** gives the household a few more years.
She copes through **spreadsheets** and planning, even when upset.

steps.text: Cancel the house plan and move the deposit into savings
Move to her parents' town where rent is half
Cancel the gym, takeaways and streaming subscriptions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's tight but you can do something with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for companies to plan properly, and they should be honest with staff. I'd say it in the team meeting. I'd want my manager to tell us what the next three years look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have three good years at Clearclaim, then trouble. I'd use those years to move closer to the insurance side, where people deal with tricky claims face to face. Fraud investigation, maybe, where you visit garages and talk to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools properly in the first year, since everyone would be using them by then. I'd take a short course in insurance fraud investigation. I'd still save for the house, but slower, and keep the cash where we can reach it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It feels like something I could actually steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why fraud investigation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I already know how claims get flagged, I write those rules. The part of insurance that stays human is going to a garage and seeing the damaged car. I'd also get out of the office, which wouldn't be bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy the house in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in year three if I've switched by then. I'd only buy once I'm in work that lasts past 2031. It's annoying, but it's sensible.

say: I'd say companies should **plan properly** and be **honest** with staff.
I'd ask my manager what the **next three years** look like.
think: I privately expect **three good years** at Clearclaim, then trouble.
I'd move toward **fraud investigation**, where people visit garages face to face.
do: Learn the **AI tools** properly in year one.
Take a short course in **insurance fraud investigation**.
Keep saving for the **house**, but slower, with cash within reach.
feel: She feels **anxious** but able to **steer** it.
S3.quote: The part of insurance that stays human is going to a garage and seeing the damaged car.
fieldNote: She uses her **claims rules** knowledge as a bridge to fraud work.

Five years turns alarm into a **plan she can steer**.

steps.text: Learn Clearclaim's AI tools properly in the first year
Take a short course in insurance fraud investigation
Keep saving for the house more slowly, with cash easy to reach

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough for us to buy the house first, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare, so let's not panic but let's not waste it. I'd say companies and colleges should start the retraining now. That's about as political as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the job still goes, just later. Ten years means I can buy a house, pay down a chunk of it, and move into something steadier before 2036. It's still a lot of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house in the next two or three years, while my job is solid. I'd learn the AI tools as the team does. Around 2030 I'd start the move into fraud or claims investigation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but at the low end. More like a long to-do list than a fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd take on a mortgage knowing the job ends by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because rent goes up forever and a mortgage at least ends. If I've paid down seven or eight years by 2036, that's a much better spot than renting with nothing. Marco agrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a student starting computer science now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a student starting computer science now to pick something with people in it as well. Pair the coding with a field, like health or insurance. Pure coding is the bit that goes.

say: I'd say **don't panic**, but don't **waste** the decade either.
I'd say companies and colleges should start **retraining** now.
think: I privately expect the **job still goes**, just later.
Ten years lets me **buy and pay down** a house before 2036.
do: Buy a **house** with Marco in the next two or three years.
Learn the **AI tools** at the same pace as the team.
feel: She feels low-level **anxiety**, more a long **to-do list** than a fire.
S4.quote: Rent goes up forever and a mortgage at least ends.
fieldNote: More warning makes her **buy sooner**, betting on paying the loan down early.
She'd advise students to **pair coding** with another field.
Her centre outlook shows in calls for **steady preparation** over protest.

steps.text: Buy a house with Marco in the next two or three years
Learn the AI tools at the same pace as her team

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it lands before we'd even have the deposit. What would help is a clear warning from my employer and help with retraining, and maybe help for first-time buyers so people like us aren't stuck renting forever.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about partners. People talk about jobs like we live alone, but everything I decide is with my boyfriend Marco.

headlineQuote: People talk about jobs like we live alone, but everything I decide is with my boyfriend Marco.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old** developer writing **claims rules** for car insurance software.
She lives with Marco, a cook, and their life plans centre on a **house deposit**.
She uses AI **now and then** and would become the checker of AI-written rules.
Fast AGI **alarms** her and cancels the house; slower AGI pushes her toward **fraud investigation**.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it lands **before the deposit** is ready.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **warning from employers** and help with retraining.
Support for **first-time buyers** so couples aren't stuck renting.
